title: Pork and Cabbage Jiaozi
subtitle: boiled dumplings with pork mince and napa cabbage
excerpt: Handmade dumplings filled with seasoned pork and napa cabbage, folded and boiled until plump and tender. A northern Chinese tradition made for gatherings and celebrations. Makes 40 dumplings.
sourceNotes: Jiaozi are one of the oldest and most widespread foods in China, with written references dating to the Han dynasty. The boiled pork and cabbage version is the most common form in northern China, particularly in Beijing, Shandong and Manchuria. They are a central part of Chinese New Year celebrations, traditionally eaten at midnight on New Year's Eve, and are documented extensively in Chinese culinary literature across the twentieth century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked dumplings on a tray, then transfer to bags. Cook from frozen in boiling water for 10 to 12 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Fill and fold the dumplings up to 4 hours ahead, covered in the fridge. Do not freeze if the skins have been made from scratch and are very thin.

glossaryTerms.definition: Chinese dumplings with a thin wheat dough wrapper and a savoury filling, typically pork with vegetables. They can be boiled, steamed or pan-fried (guotie). Boiled jiaozi are the most common form in northern China.

A large, pale-leafed cabbage with a mild, slightly sweet flavour. Also called Chinese cabbage or wombok. When salted and squeezed for dumpling filling, it loses moisture and becomes tender without becoming watery.
A Chinese rice wine with a nutty, amber flavour used widely in marinades, sauces and braises. Named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. Dry sherry is the closest substitute.
Finely milled maize starch used to thicken sauces and coat ingredients before frying. In dumpling fillings it helps bind moisture. Mixed with cold water before adding to a hot pan to avoid lumps.

content.text: This recipe makes 40
jiaozi
and takes about 90 minutes from start to finish.
Napa cabbage
is salted and squeezed dry before mixing with seasoned pork mince,
Shaoxing wine
and
cornflour
. Bought round dumpling wrappers work well; homemade dough is better.
Squeezing every drop of water from the cabbage is the most important step. Watery filling makes the wrappers soggy and the dumplings split during boiling.
What you need

items.prepNote: round dumpling wrappers, or make your own from 300 g plain flour and 150 ml just-boiled water

content.text: Method
Toss the shredded napa cabbage with 1 tsp salt and leave for 15 minutes. Squeeze out as much water as possible with your hands, then wrap in a clean tea towel and wring again.

Combine the squeezed cabbage with the pork mince, ginger, spring onions, Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, sesame oil, cornflour and white pepper. Stir in one direction for 2 minutes until the mixture comes together and feels slightly sticky.
Place a wrapper on a clean surface. Put 1 heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre. Dampen the edges with water, fold in half and press to seal, pleating the edge if you like.
Repeat with the remaining wrappers and filling. Place finished dumplings on a lightly floured tray.
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add dumplings in batches of 15 to 20. Stir gently to prevent sticking.
When the water returns to the boil, add 150 ml cold water. Repeat twice more (three additions of cold water in total). The dumplings are done when they float and look plump, about 8 minutes total.
Remove with a slotted spoon. Mix the dipping sauce and serve alongside.

items.cause: Wrapper is too thin, or the filling was too wet.
items.fix: Squeeze the cabbage very dry and seal the edges firmly with damp fingers. Do not overfill.

items.cause: Insufficient seasoning in the raw mix, which tastes milder than once cooked.
items.fix: Fry a small teaspoon of filling in a pan and taste it before wrapping. Adjust soy sauce or sesame oil.

items.cause: The water was not at a rolling boil when they went in.
items.fix: Make sure the water is boiling vigorously and stir gently right after adding the dumplings.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Jiaozi are eaten across northern China, above all at Chinese New Year and the winter solstice. Families fold dumplings together at the table. The same filling can be boiled, steamed, or pan-fried. Pan-fried jiaozi are called guotie or potstickers. The pleat shape varies by region and by habit. Imperfect crimping still tastes the same.
